catalog_quote: This chapter gives an overview of tone in Sheko, including its functions, its realisation, and its distribution. Sheko has four level tonemes. These play a role in the lexicon and in the grammar. The levels are numbered from 1 (lowest) to 4 (highest). ... Tone in Sheko has a lexical as well as a grammatical functional load. Tone can be characterized as follows: On the whole, tone in Sheko appears as stable. There is no downstep (not to be expected with four levels of height). One of the major functions of tone is to distinguish between persons. This distinction is found with pronouns, possessor prefixes and verbal subject clitics. ... All verbs can be classified H or L. Tone on verb stems in the TAM paradigms is predictable once the lexical tone class is known. The two classes cover the range of four levels of tone in inflection. ... new_statements.relation_note: The listed open URL (the Harvard library catalogue docid.._item_2960388) resolves to Leiden Scholarly Publications item 2960388, which is Hellenthal's 2010 dissertation 'A grammar of Sheko', not the 2023 Oxford Handbook chapter; the OUP handbook DOI landing could not be reached by automated download, so the 2023 chapter itself was not obtained (two attempts used: Leiden landing -> PDF; OUP DOI). The 2010 grammar is already the catalog's source ( : classification tonal-OR-pitch accent, built from the font-scrambled LOT copy decoded by cipher). The Leiden copy has a clean text layer and confirms that record word for word on the same printed pages (111, 113): four level tonemes, lexical+gramma…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Sheko is described as a four-level register-tone language (tonemes 1-4 on every tone-bearing unit, i.e. vowel or syllabic nasal), with lexical tone on nouns and H/L lexical tone classes on verbs whose surface level is set by the TAM paradigm. The grammar contains no stress or accent section and never uses the words 'stress' or 'accent' as prosodic terms (whole-text search of the clean Leiden text layer: 0 hits for 'accent', the only 'stress' string is 'distress'; 'prominent' only about dialectal allophones and TAM categories; 'intonation' only for the interrogative final fall).
new_statements.exceptions: none about stress; tonal notes: no downstep; question intonation is a final falling contour (sec. 4.1, 13.3); sec. 8.1.1 'Prosodical and morphological markedness' concerns gemination/lengthening/reduplication in ideophones, not stress
new_statements.identity_note: Hellenthal 2010 covers the Sheko language of the Sheko and Guraferda districts (SNNPR, Ethiopia) and notes a Sheko vs. Guraferda dialect difference in consonant allophones (p. 47-48); the tone description is for Sheko proper. Not to be confused with shek1244 Shekkacho (Kafa/Gonga), a different language.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification 'tonal' rests on the standard and only reference grammar of Sheko (Hellenthal 2010, 517 pp.), held as the publisher's open-access PDF; the deciding quotation is verbatim at the stated pages (confirmed in the decoded text and on the rendered image of printed p.111; the second reader had also checked pp.113/127 images). The grammar describes four level tonemes with lexical and grammatical load and contains no stress/accent statement (a full-text search for stress/accent confirms). Older phonologies (Aklilu 1988, 1996) differ only in positing three tones, per the grammar's own review (p.112). Nothing in the Glottolog bibliography is a better or contrary source; the 2023 handbook sketch is by the same author. Only improvement: the strength of the evidence 'publisher-text' is conservative given page-image verification — could be raised to page-image-backed. no reclassification.
